Rehearsed
re-hĕrst'
v. (past tense of rehearse: to recount in order; to repeat what was said or done)
Old French rehercier, to harrow over again, from herce, a harrow — to go back over the same ground. In the Authorized Version it never means practice; it always means to recount.

Biblical Definition

To rehearse in the Authorized Version is to lay a matter out in order before someone who has a right to hear it. Samuel, having heard Israel's demand for a king, “rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD” (1Sa 8:21) — the prophet's first act with bad news was to take it, word for word, to God. When David's words about the Philistine were reported, “they rehearsed them before Saul” (1Sa 17:31). Then twice in Acts, at moments of decision. Challenged by the circumcision party for eating with Gentiles, “Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order unto them” (Act 11:4) — no argument from authority, no appeal to his office; he simply laid out what God had done, in sequence, and the objection died. Returning from the first missionary journey, Paul and Barnabas gathered the church and “rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles” (Act 14:27). The pattern is worth marking: the apostolic answer to controversy was narrative testimony, ordered and verifiable, of what God had actually done.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to rehearse as to repeat; to recite; to relate; to tell over; to recount or narrate in order.

expand to see more

REHEARSE, v.t. To repeat; to recite; to utter or narrate again what has been said or written.

2. To relate; to tell; to recount; to narrate in order.

REHEARSED, pp. Repeated; recited; narrated; told over.

Key Scripture

1Sa 8:21 — "And Samuel heard all the words of the people, and he rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD."

Act 11:4 — "But Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order unto them, saying,"

Act 14:27 — "And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles."

Modern Corruption

Where Scripture rehearses what God has done, the modern report rehearses what the workers have achieved — numbers, reach, momentum — and the grammar of the sentence quietly changes the subject.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply narrowed in ordinary English to mean practising a performance, which is a real loss but not a corruption. What is worth recovering is the discipline the biblical usage describes. Acts 14:27 gives the apostolic missionary report in a single sentence, and every noun in it belongs to God: they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles. Compare the ordinary shape of a modern ministry report, in which the subject of the sentences is generally the ministry — what we launched, what we reached, what we grew — with God appearing in a clause of thanks at the end. The difference is not modesty; it is theology. Peter in Acts 11:4 faced a genuine church crisis and answered it by rehearsing the matter from the beginning and expounding it by order, and the record says his hearers held their peace and glorified God. A church would be strengthened by recovering both halves of that practice: bad news carried first into the ears of the LORD, as Samuel carried it, and good news reported with God as the subject of the verbs.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar (H1696), to speak, to declare; Greek ektithemi (G1620), to set forth in order, to expound; Greek anangello (G312), to report, to declare fully.

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak, to declare, to recount; Samuel repeating Israel's words in the ears of the LORD; 1 Samuel 8:21.

Greek ektithemi (G1620) — to set out, to expound in order; Peter's orderly account at Jerusalem and Priscilla and Aquila expounding the way to Apollos; Acts 11:4, 18:26.

Greek anangello (G312) — to report, to declare fully what has been seen; the missionary report at Antioch; Acts 14:27, 15:4.

Usage

"“He rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD” — bad news carried first to God."

"“Peter rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order” — controversy answered with ordered testimony."

"“Rehearsed all that God had done with them” — the missionary report with God as the subject."
